source: KDT8 ch2, ch3, ch5, ch71; Sarkar OCR; Katzung16 ch66; NMC guideline 2022; unsourced items marked

cards.front: Short note: Parts of a prescription

points: Prescriber address (letter pad with name and address); signature with registration number
Date of writing
Patient name, age, sex and address
Superscription: Rx
Inscription: drug name and strength; no abbreviations
Subscription: instructions to the pharmacist (compounding, quantity to supply)
Directions to the patient: quantity, frequency, time, route and other relevant instructions
Common abbreviations include o.d., b.d., t.i.d., h.s., stat, s.o.s., p.o. and a.c.

cards.front: Prescription criticism: what is your checklist?
cards.back: Legibility and completeness (prescriber, patient, date, signature); generic names; each drug justified by the diagnosis; correct dose, frequency, route and duration; no unnecessary drugs, tonics or irrational fixed-dose combinations; no interacting or contraindicated drugs; no unsafe abbreviations; injection only when oral is unsuitable; cost; and patient instructions.

cards.front: Classify: types of irrational prescribing
cards.text: {{Under-prescribing}} (needed drug not given, or dose/duration too small); {{over-prescribing}} (drug not indicated, or too long or too much); {{incorrect (inappropriate) prescribing}} (wrong diagnosis, ignores allergy or interactions); {{extravagant prescribing}} (costly drug when a cheaper equal one exists); {{multiple prescribing}} (two or more drugs for the same effect).

cards.front: Give common irrationalities seen in prescriptions.
cards.back: Antibiotics for viral fever or nonspecific diarrhoea; routine vitamins and tonics; drugs unrelated to the diagnosis (e.g. a PPI for any abdominal symptom); wrong drug (a beta-blocker for an asthmatic with hypertension); doubtful drugs (cough mixtures, memory enhancers); injections when oral will do; wrong dose or duration; needless combinations (ciprofloxacin + tinidazole for every diarrhoea); costly newer drugs; corticosteroids for fever; polypharmacy.

cards.front: Short note: P-drug concept

points: The personal drug a doctor has chosen to prescribe regularly for a given indication and knows well
Includes drug, dosage form, dosage schedule and duration
Differs between countries and doctors (cost, availability, formularies)
Define the diagnosis
Specify the therapeutic objective
List the effective drug groups
Choose a group by efficacy, safety, suitability and cost
Choose the P-drug (substance, dosage form, schedule, duration)
Newest and costliest is not always safest or best
Builds pharmacological knowledge and awareness of alternatives
Patient safety rests with the prescriber, not with seniors or sales representatives

cards.front: Essay: Choosing a P-drug for an acute attack of angina (WHO example)

points: Exertional chest pain relieved by rest: angina pectoris (classify stable/unstable, classic/variant)
Coronary stenosis cannot be dilated by drugs, so reduce myocardial oxygen demand quickly
Ways: lower preload, contractility, heart rate or afterload
Nitrates, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers
Efficacy and safety broadly similar
Suitability decides: the patient must treat the attack alone, and only nitrates come as sublingual tablets or oromucosal spray
Nitrates are cheap generics
Glyceryl trinitrate, isosorbide mononitrate and dinitrate do not differ in efficacy or safety, so cost decides
Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate tablet; a second tablet after 5-10 minutes if pain persists, then see a doctor
Prescribe a small supply because the drug is volatile

cards.front: P-drug versus P-treatment: what is the difference?
cards.back: Not every problem needs a drug. P-treatment can be advice, non-drug treatment, a drug, referral, or a mix. In simple constipation the first P-treatment is advice (fluids, fibre, exercise); a laxative such as senna is kept for severe short-term cases, and persistent cases need investigation.

cards.front: What are the WHO steps for improving rational prescribing?
cards.back: 1) Identify the patient's problem. 2) Make the diagnosis. 3) List possible drug and non-drug treatments and choose on efficacy, convenience and safety. 4) Start treatment with a complete, accurate prescription. 5) Give information and warnings. 6) Monitor the outcome (passively by the patient, or actively at a follow-up visit).

cards.front: When is a fixed-dose combination (FDC) rational? Give examples.
cards.back: When the patient needs every component in the amounts present. Advantages: convenience, adherence and sometimes cost; synergy (sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim, levodopa + carbidopa); additive effect with different side effects (amlodipine + atenolol); one component offsetting another's side effect (thiazide + potassium-sparing diuretic); and preventing monotherapy in TB, HIV and falciparum malaria.

cards.front: Complete: disadvantages of fixed-dose combinations
cards.text: The patient may not need {{all the components}}; the dose of one cannot be {{adjusted}} without changing the other; components may have different {{durations of action}}; renal or hepatic disease may affect the components {{differently}}; an adverse effect cannot be {{attributed to one drug}}; a contraindication to one contraindicates {{the whole product}}.

cards.front: Essay: Judging the rationality of a given fixed-dose combination (exam approach)

points: Is every component actually needed by the patient, in an appropriate amount?
Is any combination banned in India (listed in KDT8 Appendix-4)?
Do the components act by different mechanisms so that benefits add up while side effects do not?
Does one component counter a side effect of another?
Is the combination truly synergistic?
Antimicrobial combinations should be avoided
Corticosteroids should never be combined with any other drug meant for internal use
Rational or irrational, with reasons and a better alternative

cards.front: How does Schedule Y group fixed-dose combinations for approval?
cards.back: Group 1: one or more ingredients is a new drug (handled like any new drug). Group 2: approved drugs combined for the first time with likely PK or PD interaction (needs data and trials in India). Group 3: marketed FDC with a new ratio or new claim (needs rationale and trials). Group 4: ingredients long used together without expected interaction (no new animal or human data).

cards.front: Which drug class should never be in a fixed-dose combination for internal use?
cards.back: Corticosteroids.

cards.front: Complete: basic pharmacokinetic formulae
cards.text: Volume of distribution V = {{dose given i.v. / plasma concentration}}; clearance CL = {{rate of elimination / plasma concentration}}; elimination rate constant k = {{CL / V}}; half-life t½ = {{0.693 x V / CL}}.

cards.front: Loading dose: formula and what governs it.
cards.back: Loading dose = target plasma concentration x V / F. It depends only on volume of distribution (and bioavailability), not on clearance or half-life. Used when a long-t½ drug must act quickly (digoxin, amiodarone, chloroquine).

cards.front: Maintenance dose rate: formula and what governs it.
cards.back: Maintenance dose rate = target steady-state concentration x CL / F. It depends on clearance (and so on t½). Doubling the dose rate doubles the average steady-state concentration in first-order kinetics.

cards.front: How long does it take to reach steady state on repeated dosing?
cards.back: About 4 to 5 half-lives (plateau principle). A new steady state after a change in dose rate also takes 4 to 5 half-lives. Smaller, more frequent doses reduce the swing between peak and trough.

cards.front: Worked problem: 60 kg patient; target Cpss 6 mg/L; F 0.7; V 1.4 L/kg; CL 80 mL/h/kg. Loading and daily maintenance dose?
cards.back: V = 1.4 x 60 = 84 L; CL = 0.08 x 60 = 4.8 L/h. Loading dose = 6 x 84 / 0.7 = 720 mg. Maintenance = 6 x 4.8 / 0.7 = about 41 mg/h, or about 987 mg/day.

cards.front: How is a dose revised from a measured plasma level?
cards.back: For a drug with first-order kinetics: new dose rate = previous dose rate x target Cpss / measured Cpss.

cards.front: First-order versus zero-order elimination: what is the difference?
cards.back: First order: a constant fraction is removed per unit time and clearance is constant (most drugs). Zero order: a constant amount is removed per unit time because elimination is saturated, so clearance falls as concentration rises (ethanol). Phenytoin, theophylline, tolbutamide and warfarin can switch to zero order at higher doses, so levels rise out of proportion to dose.

cards.front: How is an individual or child dose calculated from the adult dose?
cards.back: By body weight: dose = body weight (kg) / 70 x average adult dose. By body surface area: dose = BSA (m2) / 1.7 x adult dose, with BSA from the Dubois formula or a nomogram. Age-based formulae are no longer used; mg/kg dosing is preferred, and BSA dosing is used mainly for anticancer drugs.

cards.front: Worked example: 1000 mg given i.v. gives a plasma concentration of 50 mg/L. What is V?
cards.back: V = dose / concentration = 1000 mg / 50 mg/L = 20 L. It is an apparent volume: the volume that would hold all the drug at the plasma concentration.

cards.front: Statistics exercise: which test for which data?
cards.back: Two independent group means: unpaired t test. Same subjects before and after: paired t test. More than two group means: ANOVA. Proportions or counts in categories: chi-square test. Data not normally distributed or ordinal: the non-parametric counterpart.

cards.front: Degrees of freedom for unpaired and paired t tests.
cards.back: Unpaired: n1 + n2 - 2. Paired: n - 1.

cards.front: Worked example: case-control study of smoking and lung cancer. Cases 50 smokers, 10 non-smokers; controls 10 smokers, 50 non-smokers. Odds ratio?
cards.back: Odds of exposure in cases = 50/10 = 5; in controls = 10/50 = 0.2. OR = 5/0.2 = 25 (equivalently ad/bc). OR above 1 means exposure is positively associated with disease; association does not prove causation.

cards.front: Worked example: a drug cuts mortality of a disease from 50% to 25%. What is the NNT?
cards.back: Absolute reduction = 0.50 - 0.25 = 0.25, so NNT = 1 / 0.25 = 4: four patients must be treated to save one life. The same halving of mortality in a rarely fatal disease gives a much larger NNT.

cards.front: Standard deviation versus standard error of the mean: how are they related?
cards.back: SD describes the spread of individual observations. SEM describes how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean: SEM = SD / square root of n, so it falls as sample size rises.

cards.front: Drug-interaction exercise: how do you work through a given pair?
cards.back: Name the object and precipitant drug; classify the mechanism (pharmaceutical, pharmacokinetic: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion; or pharmacodynamic); state the clinical result; then manage it: avoid the pair, separate doses, adjust dose, or monitor. A possible interaction does not always forbid joint use.

cards.front: Classify: drugs most likely to cause clinically important interactions
cards.text: Drugs with a {{narrow safety margin}} (aminoglycosides, digoxin, lithium); drugs controlling {{closely regulated functions}} (antihypertensives, antidiabetics, anticoagulants); {{highly plasma protein bound}} drugs (NSAIDs, oral anticoagulants, sulfonylureas); drugs with {{saturation kinetics}} (phenytoin, theophylline).

cards.front: Give examples of in-vitro (pharmaceutical) incompatibilities.
cards.back: Penicillin G or ampicillin mixed with gentamicin; thiopentone with succinylcholine or morphine; heparin with penicillin, gentamicin or hydrocortisone; noradrenaline in sodium bicarbonate solution. Avoid mixing parenteral drugs in one syringe or infusion.

cards.front: Exercise: tetracycline taken with an antacid or iron. Mechanism and management?
cards.back: Insoluble complexes form in the gut, so tetracycline absorption falls. Give the two drugs 2 to 3 hours apart so they do not meet in the gut.

cards.front: What do the NMC short exercises include?
cards.back: Interpreting the results of a previous tracing (table exercise) and demonstrating or interpreting drug effects in humans; small-animal experiments are optional, as regulations allow. The exercises are observed and assessed.

cards.front: Tracing exercise: what do you look for in a given kymograph or physiograph record?
cards.back: Baseline, dose cycle and responses; rising responses with dose (graded DRC); a parallel right shift with a competitive antagonist versus a fall in the maximum with a noncompetitive one; and falling responses with repeated doses (tachyphylaxis). Tabulate the responses and plot them against log dose.

cards.front: Computer-assisted learning (CAL) and simulated experiments: why are they used?
cards.back: CAL and simulated experiments can replace some live-animal practicals under the 3Rs. They cut cost and animal use, let students repeat an experiment and give clear results. They cannot fully copy real biological variation. The NMC expects DRC and agonist-antagonist experiments on simulations and CAL in teaching.

cards.front: Which human-volunteer test does the NMC list for drugs affecting psychomotor function?
cards.back: The critical flicker fusion test, done under supervision, along with tests of memory, pain, cardiovascular and respiratory function.

cards.front: What are the 3Rs in animal experimentation, and what fourth R is added?
cards.back: Replacement, reduction and refinement of animal use. Rehabilitation is the added fourth R, a measure for the care of the animals.

cards.front: Who approves experiments on animals in an Indian institution?
cards.back: Experiments on animals are approved by the institutional animal ethics committee (IAEC). CPCSEA controls the IAEC under Government of India guidelines.

cards.front: Formula method: what is the dose equation?
cards.back: D/H x Q = X. D = dose desired, H = dose on hand, Q = quantity or form on hand, X = amount to give.

cards.front: Ratio-proportion method: how do you set up the proportion?
cards.back: Dosage on hand / amount on hand = dosage desired / X (amount to give). Cross-multiply to solve for X.

cards.front: What are the three steps the book teaches for dosage calculation?
cards.back: 1) Convert to the same system and same-size units. 2) Consider whether the dose is reasonable. 3) Calculate with the formula method.

cards.front: IV drip rate in gtt/min: which formula?
cards.back: V (mL) / T (min) x C (gtt/mL) = R (gtt/min). Total mL / total min x 60 min/h gives mL/h.

cards.front: Shortcut from an infusion rate in mL/h to gtt/min?
cards.back: Divide the mL/h rate by the drop factor constant. The result is R in gtt/min.

cards.front: Give the Celsius-Fahrenheit conversion formulas.
Acetaminophen for fever in a child: what does the book give as the dose and limit?
cards.back: 10 to 15 mg/kg by mouth every 4 hours, and not more than 5 doses per day.

cards.front: Amoxicillin for a child: what dose range is printed?
cards.back: The label gives 20 to 40 mg/kg/day in divided doses every 8 hours. The question states 40 mg/kg/day in divided doses q.8h as the reference dose.
